Press Release:


Dr Andrew Ross
How did a doctor working in a vast impoverished area fund a bursary scheme to achieve the impossible...making medical professionals of over 200 rural youngsters? Carte Blanche meets the inspiring Dr Andrew Ross - recipient of a prestigious presidential Baobab Award - and the young medics he never gave up on, now back home and serving in their community.


Script:


Dr Andrew Ross, Umthombo and the Baobab award - Script

Andrew: I look back and I’m a bit amazed in fact

In 2002 Dr Andrew Ross set his sights on an impossible dream.

Andrew: I’m amazed that students have some out of the woodwork, I’m amazed that we get so many successes, so many people pass, I’m more amazed than proud of this thing”

Last year, Dr Ross received the Order of the Boabab - a presidential award, for his bold initiative

Andrew: And in terms of the award, I’m amazed that they considered something like this in a sense it’s a little part of south Africa and we are doing something with a relatively small number of students in the scheme of things

He began by setting up a bursary scheme in a vast impoverished area on the border of Mozambique.

Bheki: Growing up in this area hasn’t been easy, you grew up bathing in the dams or rivers and your parents couldn’t even afford to buy you shoes to go to school with

Bheki was one of nine siblings living in a remote part of the district

Bheki: You are bound to grow up looking after cattle, you are bound to grow up doing the stick fighting, you grew up living isolated from everything, you don’t know anything outside of that

The project based at Mosvold hospital offered Bheki a way out

Andrew: When I first got to Mosvold there were five doctors working there, three from England and two South Aricans

Mosvold hospital serves a community of over 100 000 people. In 2002 they were down to 2 permanent staff members.

Andrew: In 1992 three indicated that they would be leaving, then there were just the two of us in a 250 bed hospital. Kinda like aahh-ok”

Dr Ross was told that the staffing challenge was his to solve, and so he resolved to invest in the local youth.

Andrew: We kinda thought well I wonder if it’s possible, I wonder if it’s possible this would be great, if we could train them to be health care professionals it’ would solve a whole lot of issues.

From the start the odds were stacked against them.

Andrew: Ingwavuma schools are really really really bad.

Bheki: When you doing experiments we didn’t have a laboratory then I would try and imagine some of those things

Andrew: And people also said to me, youv’e heard about the pass rated at university, people just aren't gonna make it. So, instead of taking all the advice we decided, I think I was a bit mad at the time, lt's worth a try.

I never thought I would study reach grade 12 and then go to the university, that for me was.... cause I’d never seen anyone doing that around the community. The norm was for me you go to the mines or you go to the farms

Sipamandla had never considered a world beyond Ingwavuma. His father left them for the mines, and his mother struggled to support them by selling sweets and vegetables. She had little formal education.

My mom went up to standard three or so. But she had that inspiration ‘you should go to school, you should go to school”/

He first heard about the Umthombo bursary scheme at Ingwavuma high when he was in grade 12.

So they used to come during the holdiays to do motivational talks.

Andrew: We said , however you get your marks, I don’t know. You have to get the marks and get a place and if you do that we will take you

For me it was the only hope that I had.

Bheki: For me it was OK, now that there is that chance, I want to grab it with both hands

Andrew: “so what did the kids do?” I don’t know, there’s a guy called Sipamandla Ngomomozulu, he didn’t have a maths teacher, he still got a B in higher grade in maths.

Sipamandla: I knew that I only had that chance

Andrew: You know somehow, If you put a challenge to people and you make the steps very clear there are amazing people that will step up and do amazing things

Bheki: The results came that I’m one of the people who have made it, it was, I remember myself running around the yard shouting... she said ‘are you mad?” I said “no I’m leaving, I’m no longer a farm boy I’m going to the city now”

Andrew: I think it’s a massive adjustment coming from rural Ingwavuma to being at university

Sipamandla: It was terrible, cause, I’d only been to the city once.

Bheki: That multiracial mixture there, “hey”

Dumisani: It’s a culture shock, yeah - sometime you find the students are struggling because, not of academic issue but because of cultural issues.




Dumisani Gumede coordinates a mentorship programme for the project.

Sipamandla: My language skills, my socialization skills and my levels of confidence it’s what I struggled with.

Dumisani: We used to say when we were at high school, we are leaning in Zunglish, it’s a mixture of English and Zulu, but when you get to university, there is no Zunglish, there is only English.

Sipamandla: So I had to study study study study.

Sipimandla struggled when he first went to university, but by the end of his second year he was the top student in the arts faculty.

Sipamandla: So then I had that pressure that now becasue I was the top student, Dr Ross said you must keep that pace.

At the time, the project only had funding for the first year of study.

Andrew: I had R30 000 in the bank, we kind of said, Ok, we gonna do this, if it kills us we gonna try and do this, we gonna try and find the money.

In 2007 Umthombo received a million rand grant from the Discovery foundation.

Andrew: I think initially they believed in us, when we did’t have very much to show for it, except a story and lotsof enthusiasm and a belief that it was important.

Today Umthombo supports 234 health studies students and boasts a 90% pass rate.

Bheki: That moment, key moment was when I get the results with degree completed!

Bheki qualified as an optometrist and headed for home

Bheki: I wanted to come and work here because this is where I grew up, so I felt that no, I wouldn't have done justice I I hadn’t come to work at Mosvold.

He set up eye clinics at Mosvold hospital and across the the district of ingwavuma.

Bheki: One thing about optometric services it that you make the change and I will see it now, it’s like you bring back life to them.

Sipamandla went on to achieve his masters in Clinical Psychology and is setting up mental health services across the district.

Sipamandla: I was working with the people who were appreciative of the services and who really needed the services

He has affected real change in the area both professionally and personally.

Sipamandla: I have managed to build my mom a house, it’s not only just a way to say thank you. I could go back and point ‘that’s my family” I think she’s completely humbled, I can see she’s the happiest happiest mum ever.

Sipamandla is one of 218 Umthombo graduates working in local hospitals today.

Andrew: It’s unbelievable, in some ways we see it as a miracle, you know, ti’s a miracle that we could find people, that we found the money along the way. Ja, I would say it’s a miracle.
